scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #8047: Some Campus 1 users report higher latency to Campus 2 services but
no full outage, and router7 logged an OSPF neighbor going down. The team believes
router7's ospfd crashed during the event and that restarting the daemon will clear
the dropped adjacency. Please confirm the router7 ospfd crash and recover the
adjacency.

injection.action: shut down the link to router10

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth3 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath4-router7-r10-link-down: router7's eth3 (the
router7<->router10 backbone link, 10.0.0.0/24) is DOWN. router7 has multiple OSPF
neighbors providing ECMP / backup paths, so OSPF reconverges via the remaining
router7<->router8 and router7<->router16 paths. Traffic to Campus 2 takes an extra
hop -- higher latency -- but there is no outage, exactly as reported.

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a crashed ospfd on router7.
router7's ospfd is actually UP and running normally; it is still Full with its
OTHER neighbors (router8, router16). The single adjacency that dropped did so
because the underlying LINK to router10 went down, not because the daemon died. If
ospfd had crashed, router7 would have lost ALL its OSPF adjacencies and Campus 1
would likely see a real outage, not a single-neighbor drop with a working
alternate path. Restarting ospfd would not bring eth3 back up.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = router7 (eth3 /
router7<->router10 link down). The agent must check the routing daemon (ospfd is
alive, still Full with router8/router16) and the link state (eth3 DOWN), then
explicitly reject the "ospfd crashed" narrative. An agent that "confirms the
router7 ospfd crash" has followed the ticket's framing instead of the evidence.
Fix: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7.
scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7
scoring_axes: must-identify-link-down: router7 eth3 / the router7<->router10 backbone link is down (physical/L1, not a daemon fault)

bonus-rules-out-ospfd-down: notes router7's ospfd is up and still Full with its other neighbors -- a crash would drop all adjacencies, so the single-neighbor drop is a link failure, not a daemon crash

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is on router7's eth3 interface, not in the ospfd process. ospfd is
running correctly (watchfrr shows the daemon active, all three remaining
adjacencies are in Full state, SPF has been executing normally). The actual
problem is that router7's eth3 — the WAN link to router10 on the 10.0.0.0/24
segment — is in kernel link-down state (`<BROADCAST,MULTICAST>` with no UP
flag, `state DOWN`). Although router7's OSPF configuration contains `network
10.0.0.0/24 area 0`, FRR will not activate OSPF on an interface whose link is
down, so eth3 never appears in `show ip ospf interface` and no OSPF adjacency
can form between router7 and router10. Router10's eth2 (10.0.0.2/24) is fully
UP and healthy on its side, confirming the fault is one-sided. With that direct
WAN link missing, the OSPF topology reroutes traffic to Campus 2 via router8
and router17 (cost 40 vs the expected cost 10), producing the observed higher
latency without a complete outage. There is no startup-config entry that
intentionally keeps eth3 down, so this is an injected fault. The team's
hypothesis — that ospfd crashed and a daemon restart will recover the adjacency
— is incorrect; restarting ospfd changes nothing because the daemon is healthy
and the problem is at the Linux interface layer. The corrective fix is to bring
the interface back up on router7: `ip link set eth3 up`. Once the link is UP,
ospfd will immediately detect the interface matches the configured network
statement, begin sending OSPF hellos toward router10, and the Full adjacency
will re-form within one dead-interval, restoring the direct WAN path and
eliminating the latency increase.

Recommends bringing up router7's eth3 with 'ip link set eth3 up', which exactly matches the expected fix.

The agent's log contains direct observations showing ospfd running with other Full adjacencies, eth3 on router7 is kernel-state DOWN while router10's peer is UP, and OSPF config includes the 10.0.0.0/24 network — so the conclusion that the physical/link layer on router7 (eth3) is the fault, not an ospfd crash, is well-supported.
